AI.tldr: AutoOntic induces an ontology from text by canonicalizing entity and relation types, building a type hierarchy and mining domain and range constraints. Over 90 percent of its induced endpoint types align with reference classes on two Text2KGBench subsets, and knowledge graphs built with its ontology reach 88 percent retrieval accuracy on MINE.
AI.motivation: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation depends on knowledge-graph quality, but schema-free LLM extraction produces flat graphs with no type hierarchy and no domain or range constraints.
AI.method: AutoOntic canonicalizes open-vocabulary types and relations, prioritizes types using corpus-derived relation-argument profiles, and places them in a hierarchy through local LLM-adjudicated parent and child checks. Newly inserted types can trigger reassignment of existing links. The hierarchy constrains entity deduplication and supports domain and range induction. A reference-based protocol classifies induced types as exact, broader, narrower or unrelated.
AI.result: On the Wikidata-TekGen and DBpedia-WebNLG subsets of Text2KGBench, over 90 percent of induced endpoint types align semantically with reference classes across two LLM backbones. About half match exactly, and most remaining differences concern granularity. On MINE, knowledge graphs organized by the ontology reach 88 percent retrieval accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that the induced ontology aligns well with reference classes, mostly at the right granularity, and improves retrieval on MINE.

title: Faithful in Steps: Improving Generalization and Citation in RAG via Query Decomposition
summary: Retrieval-augment generation is a prevalent strategy to mitigate hallucinations of LLMs. The attributable RAG (RAGQ) generates quotes for its answers. The quotes indicate which input contexts support the RAG to derive the answers, enhancing the answer's verifiability and trustworthiness. However, existing RAGQs exhibit significant degradation when dealing with questions that require multi-hop reasoning and multi-modal understanding, suffering from over-citation, implicit entity identification failure, and poor generalization. In this paper, we propose a novel RAGQ framework, namely QDRAG. QDRAG breaks down the input question into atomic subquestions to identify the implicit entities. Then, the reranker prunes context distractors to eliminate the downstream over-citation. To facilitate query decomposition, we propose two zero-shot approaches: QD-C and QD-R, which guide the QD MLLM to decompose the question based on context knowledge and retrieval rewards, respectively. One interesting finding is that finetuning on the QD task shows better generalizability compared to directly finetuning on the downstream RAGQ task. Experiments on four multi-modal QA benchmarks demonstrate QDRAG's efficacy in grounding answers and generating faithful citations. The framework significantly outperforms all the baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tests, even surpassing Gemini-Pro.

AI.tldr: QDRAG is an attributable RAG framework for multimodal QA that decomposes questions into atomic subquestions to find implicit entities and prunes distractors with a reranker. It improves grounding and citation faithfulness on four benchmarks and surpasses Gemini-Pro.
AI.motivation: Attributable RAG degrades on multi-hop and multimodal questions, showing over-citation, failure to identify implicit entities and poor generalization.
AI.method: QDRAG breaks each question into atomic subquestions, and a reranker prunes context distractors to remove over-citation. Two zero-shot decomposition methods, QD-C and QD-R, guide a multimodal LLM to decompose questions using context knowledge and retrieval rewards, respectively.
AI.result: On four multimodal QA benchmarks, QDRAG significantly outperforms all baselines on in-domain and out-of-domain tests and surpasses Gemini-Pro. Finetuning on the decomposition task generalizes better than finetuning directly on the downstream attributable RAG task.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that query decomposition improves grounding and faithful citation in attributable RAG, and that decomposition finetuning generalizes better than direct finetuning.

title: Can We Make an LLM Dumber, or Is It Just Playing Dumb? An Empirical Study of Believable Performance Throttling
summary: A benchmark score is commonly read as a proxy for model capability. We study the inverse problem: can a model be driven to a target score, and do its failures resemble those of a naturally weaker model? We operationalize believable performance reduction along three axes: target calibration, item-difficulty structure, and error-distribution similarity to a real weak reference. We introduce CapLadder, an IRT-calibrated suite of 1,985 items spanning mathematics, code, multiple-choice reasoning, and tool use. A simple weak-teacher LoRA dial reaches unseen target levels on reasoning with a 1.9-point held-out calibration error, whereas prompting, temperature, and weight noise cannot combine comparable range and precision. Yet on multiple choice, the dial converges to an answer-token attractor: up to 97% of its newly introduced errors land on one letter, with the attractor changing from D in Qwen to A in Llama. Logit interventions identify a dominant near-constant shift: subtracting the estimated shift on held-out items recovers 52 to 59% of lost accuracy and removes the dominant attractor, while option permutation confirms that the bias tracks token position rather than option content. With high inter-annotator agreement ($\kappa=0.94$), human-coded error-category distributions nonetheless match the weak reference on reasoning (JS = 0.00), showing that local plausibility and aggregate detectability differ. Structured tool calls exhibit more natural degradation in the Qwen family (JS = 0.09), while a globally calibrated dial transfers poorly across benchmarks (14.2-point error on two usable benchmarks). Precise score control, therefore, does not imply a portable or believable reduction in skill.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether a model can be driven to a target benchmark score with failures resembling a naturally weaker model. A weak-teacher LoRA dial reaches target levels on reasoning, but on multiple choice it collapses onto one answer letter, and a logit shift removes the attractor.
AI.motivation: A benchmark score is often read as a proxy for capability, and the authors ask whether a model's score can be reduced believably, with error patterns resembling a real weaker model, and not just reduced in number.
AI.method: The authors define believable reduction along target calibration, item-difficulty structure and error-distribution similarity to a real weak reference. They introduce CapLadder, an IRT-calibrated suite of 1,985 items across mathematics, code, multiple-choice reasoning and tool use, and compare a weak-teacher LoRA dial with prompting, temperature and weight noise.
AI.result: The LoRA dial reaches unseen target levels on reasoning with a 1.9-point held-out calibration error, which prompting, temperature and weight noise cannot match. On multiple choice up to 97 percent of new errors fall on one letter (D in Qwen, A in Llama). Subtracting the estimated shift recovers 52 to 59 percent of lost accuracy. Human-coded error categories match the weak reference on reasoning (JS = 0.00), but a globally calibrated dial transfers poorly across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that precise score control does not imply a portable or believable reduction in skill.

title: VWEN: A Curated Small Language Model for Vietnamese Paraphrasing
summary: We present VWEN, a 0.8B-parameter model for Vietnamese paraphrasing at a requested level of change and for five related tasks: generating several paraphrases, simplification, gist, register transfer and paraphrase judgement. VWEN is Qwen3.5-0.8B fine-tuned on about 7k samples chosen by a four-stage pipeline: rules and deduplication, a bidirectional entailment filter, a divergence score that assigns low and high paraphrase levels, and selection for coverage and instruction-following difficulty. We compare it with paraphrase-only recipes from the same pipeline and with training on the ViSP corpus under matched and larger step budgets. On high-divergence paraphrasing, VWEN reaches a success rate (requested level reached and meaning preserved) of 0.61 against 0.46 for the ViSP model at matched compute, a difference that holds on inputs resembling ViSP. Given four times more training examples, the ViSP model closes the gap on such inputs but not on questions, which ViSP lacks and which it often turns into statements. Across all comparisons the entailment filter is the most effective stage. Training on paraphrases alone erases abilities of the base model that the multi-task data preserves.

AI.tldr: VWEN is a 0.8B-parameter Vietnamese paraphrasing model, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-0.8B on about 7k samples chosen by a four-stage pipeline. On high-divergence paraphrasing it reaches a success rate of 0.61 versus 0.46 for a ViSP-trained model at matched compute.
AI.motivation: The paper targets Vietnamese paraphrasing at a requested level of change, plus five related tasks, using a small curated training set rather than large noisy corpora.
AI.method: The four-stage pipeline applies rules and deduplication, a bidirectional entailment filter, a divergence score that assigns low and high paraphrase levels, and selection for coverage and instruction-following difficulty. The authors compare with paraphrase-only recipes from the same pipeline and with training on the ViSP corpus under matched and larger step budgets.
AI.result: On high-divergence paraphrasing, VWEN reaches a success rate (requested level reached and meaning preserved) of 0.61, against 0.46 for the ViSP model at matched compute. With four times more examples, the ViSP model closes the gap on ViSP-like inputs but not on questions. The entailment filter is the most effective stage, and paraphrase-only training erases base-model abilities that the multi-task data preserves.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that careful curation of a small multi-task dataset yields a better small Vietnamese paraphrasing model than larger paraphrase-only data.

title: When Local Definitions Are Missing: Stable Errors in Language Models
summary: Contracts, technical manuals, and online communities often give familiar words special meanings and define them in one place. A language model that reads a passage without that definition may use the usual meaning and give an answer that sounds right but is wrong. We study this with multiple-choice questions whose correct answers depend on a local definition. The questions come from a synthetic vocabulary, commercial contracts, Reddit community glossaries, and the documentation of a decentralized exchange. We ask three language models each question with and without the definition. Without using the answer key, we then test whether their repeated answers and stated confidence reveal their own errors. Separately, we give a small open model the answer key and test whether it can predict which questions larger models get wrong. We report three findings. (1) Familiar words that a source redefines cause the most errors. Models often repeat the same wrong answer, and neither repeated answers nor stated confidence reliably flag it. (2) The source definition fixes most errors on synthetic questions, but a definition drawn from the model's own prior knowledge does not. In real contracts, the source definition fixes only about half of the errors. (3) Given an answer key, a small model can rank questions by how likely larger models are to get them wrong. These results call for tests that check answers against the full source, including its local definitions.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that language models answer wrongly and confidently when a familiar word is redefined locally, and that neither repeated answers nor stated confidence reliably flags these errors. Providing the source definition fixes most synthetic errors but only about half of real contract errors.
AI.motivation: Contracts, manuals and communities often give familiar words special local meanings, and a model reading without that definition may answer with the usual meaning, sounding correct but being wrong.
AI.method: The authors use multiple-choice questions whose answers depend on a local definition, drawn from a synthetic vocabulary, commercial contracts, Reddit community glossaries and decentralized exchange documentation. They ask three models with and without the definition, test whether repeated answers and stated confidence reveal errors, and test whether a small open model with the answer key can predict which questions larger models get wrong.
AI.result: Familiar words redefined by a source cause the most errors, and models often repeat the same wrong answer, which repetition and confidence do not reliably flag. The source definition fixes most errors on synthetic questions but not from the model's own prior knowledge, and fixes only about half the errors in real contracts. A small model given the answer key can rank questions by how likely larger models are to fail them.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that evaluations should check answers against the full source, including its local definitions.

title: ChJGBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Legal Judgment Generation with Diagnostic Evaluation
comment: 25 pages, 3 figures. Published in EMNLP 2026 (main conference)
summary: With the rapid development of LLMs, increasing attention has been paid to whether they can reliably generate complete and legally valid judicial documents. This calls for a benchmark capable of evaluating whether models can accurately apply statutes and resolve outcome-critical issues, including claims, charges, penalties, and monetary obligations. However, existing benchmarks typically focus on isolated legal tasks or coarse-grained evaluation. We introduce ChJGBench, a benchmark for generating the reasoning and dispositive sections of Chinese judgments across civil, criminal, and administrative cases. Built from 3,462 real-world judgments, ChJGBench provides a case-type-aware diagnostic evaluation framework comprising 13 metric types and adopts a hybrid paradigm. Experiments reveal no uniform advantage for legal-domain models over general-purpose models, with model strengths varying across diagnostic dimensions. Performance is generally stronger on criminal cases, while civil and administrative cases continue to present substantial challenges.

AI.tldr: ChJGBench is a benchmark for generating the reasoning and dispositive sections of Chinese judgments across civil, criminal and administrative cases, built from 3,462 real-world judgments with a diagnostic framework of 13 metric types. Legal-domain models show no uniform advantage over general-purpose models, and performance is generally stronger on criminal cases than on civil and administrative ones.
AI.motivation: Existing legal benchmarks focus on isolated tasks or coarse-grained evaluation, so they do not test whether models can apply statutes and resolve outcome-critical issues such as claims, charges, penalties and monetary obligations in complete judicial documents.
AI.method: The authors build ChJGBench from 3,462 real Chinese judgments and propose a case-type-aware diagnostic evaluation framework with 13 metric types, using a hybrid evaluation paradigm.
AI.result: Legal-domain models have no uniform advantage over general-purpose models, and each model's strengths vary across diagnostic dimensions. Performance is generally stronger on criminal cases, while civil and administrative cases remain substantially challenging.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs cannot yet reliably produce legally valid judgments in civil and administrative cases, and fine-grained diagnostic evaluation reveals model-specific strengths that coarse benchmarks would hide.

title: Differential Backpack Language Models: Sense Inhibition via Signed Contextualization Weights
summary: Backpack language models predict with a strictly linear combination of non-contextual per-word sense vectors, weighted by non-negative contextualization scores. We show that non-negativity conflates two properties: the linear readout, which carries the interpretability, and the conic combination, which merely restricts it. We relax the latter by computing the sense weights with differential attention, a difference of two softmax maps with a learned per-sense gain, so context can actively inhibit a sense; we call the result a differential Backpack. At equal parameters on WikiText-103 this cuts the Backpack's perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31%, improves over the softmax Backpack at every sense count, persists with a shrinking margin up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText, and is localized at the sense layer by ablations and controls. The learned inhibition is directly interpretable (a financial context drives the river sense of bank to -0.50), and the preserved per-sense attribution predicts counterfactual removals exactly. We tested a number of combination rules, showing the linear interface is nearly free. Making the readout nonlinear gains only 0.43 perplexity points while invalidating two thirds of the decomposition. The differential Backpack's senses are also better representations, improving zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a differential Backpack language model, which computes the sense weights with differential attention so that context can actively inhibit a sense rather than only add to it. At equal parameters on WikiText-103 it cuts the perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31% and improves zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.
AI.motivation: Backpack language models restrict sense weights to be non-negative, which couples the interpretable linear readout to a conic combination that limits how context can act on senses. The authors argue these two properties should be separated.
AI.method: The non-negative contextualization scores are replaced by a difference of two softmax maps with a learned per-sense gain, so that context can suppress a sense. The linear readout over per-word sense vectors is kept, and several combination rules are tested.
AI.result: On WikiText-103 at equal parameters the method cuts the Backpack's perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31% and beats the softmax Backpack at every sense count. The advantage persists with a shrinking margin up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText. Making the readout nonlinear gains only 0.43 perplexity points while invalidating two thirds of the decomposition, and the learned inhibition is interpretable (for example, a financial context lowers the river sense of bank to -0.50).
AI.conclusion: Relaxing non-negativity keeps the interpretable linear readout while improving performance, which suggests the linear interface is nearly free and that the restriction on context-sense interaction, not the linearity, was the limitation.

title: Can Agents Relive Past Experiences? Diagnosing Event-Affect Decoupling in Affective-Episodic Retrospection
summary: As memory-augmented agents increasingly support long-term and personalized interactions, reliable recall of emotional experiences while preserving their associated affect becomes necessary. However, existing evaluations usually assess emotion accuracy and factual memory grounding separately, overlooking event-affect correspondence. In this work, we formulate Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as a task that explicitly evaluates the recovery of past events, associated affects, and their correspondence, and define Event-Affect Decoupling as a failure mode where the correct emotion is recalled but associated with the wrong episode. To diagnose Event-Affect Decoupling, we propose EM-TRACE, a stage-wise framework that decomposes AER into retrieval, affect recovery, and realization. On a controlled GoEmotions-based benchmark, Emotion-only retrieval achieves 28.65% affect recovery but retrieves the target episode for only 4.44% of queries, yielding a UAR of 24.21%. Further analysis reveals that event retrieval and affect assignment introduce distinct binding failures. These findings show that reliable AER requires grounded recall of emotional experiences, where episode retrieval, affect recovery, event-affect binding, and generation quality should be evaluated jointly. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER), a task that jointly evaluates recall of past events, their associated affects and the correspondence between them, and introduces EM-TRACE to diagnose Event-Affect Decoupling, where the correct emotion is recalled but attached to the wrong episode. On a GoEmotions-based benchmark, Emotion-only retrieval achieves 28.65% affect recovery but retrieves the target episode for only 4.44% of queries.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of memory-augmented agents measure emotion accuracy and factual memory grounding separately, which misses whether the emotion is bound to the correct event.
AI.method: EM-TRACE is a stage-wise framework that decomposes AER into retrieval, affect recovery and realization, and is applied to a controlled benchmark built on GoEmotions.
AI.result: Emotion-only retrieval reaches 28.65% affect recovery but retrieves the target episode for only 4.44% of queries, giving a UAR of 24.21%. Event retrieval and affect assignment introduce distinct binding failures.
AI.conclusion: Reliable affective-episodic recall needs episode retrieval, affect recovery, event-affect binding and generation quality to be evaluated jointly, since each stage can fail independently.

title: ALMeD: Medieval French Gold-Standard
summary: Medieval French is one of the Romance vernacular languages with a significant history of transmission and an enormous influence on other vernacular languages of the time. The sources convey valuable knowledge about all aspects of culture. The study of Medieval French has, over the last few years, increasingly benefited from NLP-based methods. There have been numerous efforts to parse medieval French; however, these efforts use corpora comprising legal texts and -- primarily -- literary texts as their foundation and training data. This means that, except for juridical resources, scientific literature is overlooked. We present ALMeD, an annotated, semantically rich corpus (work-in-progress) of medical and surgical treatises produced in medieval French, i.e., Old and Middle French, including Anglo-Norman. Our semantically disambiguated gold standard goes beyond existing resources, focusing on medical terminology, and accounts for morphological development, evolving syntactical structures and the lack of spelling normalisation in these languages.

AI.tldr: ALMeD is a work-in-progress annotated corpus of medical and surgical treatises in medieval French (Old and Middle French, including Anglo-Norman), with a semantically disambiguated gold standard focused on medical terminology. It addresses the gap that NLP resources for medieval French mostly cover legal and literary texts.
AI.motivation: Existing NLP resources and parsers for medieval French are built mainly on legal and literary corpora, so scientific literature from the period is overlooked.
AI.method: The authors annotate a corpus of medical and surgical treatises with semantic disambiguation, and the gold standard accounts for morphological development, evolving syntax and the lack of spelling normalisation.
AI.result: The abstract reports the corpus and gold standard as a work in progress and gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The resource extends computational coverage of medieval French to scientific texts and provides a basis for medical terminology work in historical languages.

title: Dynamic Block-Online Streaming ASR for Low-Resource Agglutinative Code-Switching Speech with Morphology-Aware Evaluation
comment: Published at Interspeech 2026 (oral). 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Code: this https URL
summary: Low-resource, agglutinative languages challenge low-latency ASR, as fixed lookahead windows fail when grapheme order diverges, suffixes cross code-switch boundaries, or code-switching data is imbalanced. We present the first comprehensive study of streaming ASR for intra-sentential Bangla-English code-switching, identifying a mismatch between strict causal streaming and long-range morphological dependencies. We introduce a Dynamic Block-Online framework with VAD-aligned inference that balances semantics, latency, and context, enabling global bidirectional attention to preserve morphological integrity. To mitigate data scarcity, we propose Script-Anchored Loanword Injection, augmenting training text with English loanwords to model phonotactic transitions. We introduce CS-WER to diagnose switch, root, and suffix errors, and show that flexible latency budgets enhance recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech, with successful transfer to menstrual-medical domains.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a Dynamic Block-Online streaming ASR framework with VAD-aligned inference for intra-sentential Bangla-English code-switching, together with Script-Anchored Loanword Injection for data augmentation and a CS-WER metric that diagnoses switch, root and suffix errors. Flexible latency budgets improve recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech, with transfer to menstrual-medical domain speech.
AI.motivation: Fixed lookahead windows in low-latency ASR fail for agglutinative languages where suffixes cross code-switch boundaries, grapheme order diverges, and code-switching data is imbalanced.
AI.method: The Dynamic Block-Online framework aligns inference with voice activity detection and enables global bidirectional attention to preserve morphology. Script-Anchored Loanword Injection augments training text with English loanwords to model phonotactic transitions.
AI.result: The abstract reports that flexible latency budgets enhance recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech and transfer successfully to menstrual-medical domain speech, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Strict causal streaming conflicts with long-range morphological dependencies, and allowing flexible latency with bidirectional context helps streaming ASR for low-resource code-switched speech.

title: Outside the Purview of the Reward: Capability Drift in Multilingual Post-Training
comment: Accepted at the Foundations of LLM Post-Training in Changing Environments, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Post-training can improve rewarded behavior while weakening capabilities users still need. We study two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model. The released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, while XQuAD-English improves under the same scoring rule. An independently trained sibling adds Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping. It recovers the regressing Indic task scores and preserves MATH, but does not restore script compliance and trades off competition mathematics and code. In a later round, judge training is followed by a sharp extraction decline from the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from its earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. A MATH score decomposition associates most of the measured gain with increased boxed-answer emission; accuracy among boxed answers changes little. These results show why benchmark scores should be read alongside the response forms they reward.

AI.tldr: In a multilingual mixture-of-experts model trained with GRPO, the released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, and reward-free distillation from an earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. The paper argues that benchmark scores should be read together with the response forms they reward.
AI.motivation: Post-training optimises rewarded behaviour but can silently weaken capabilities users still need, such as Indic-language answering, and this is not visible from reward-aligned benchmarks alone.
AI.method: The authors compare two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint, one independently trained sibling with Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping, and a later round in which judge training is followed by distillation from an earlier Indic-branch checkpoint. They also decompose the MATH score.
AI.result: The released branch gains 36.07 MATH points but loses 19.32 XQuAD-Indic F1 points, while XQuAD-English improves. The sibling recovers Indic task scores and preserves MATH but does not restore script compliance. Distillation restores most of the lost F1. Most of the MATH gain is associated with increased boxed-answer emission, and accuracy among boxed answers changes little.
AI.conclusion: Apparent gains on a benchmark can come mainly from changes in answer format rather than correctness, so evaluations should inspect the response forms that training rewards.

title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
summary: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper offers a survey and taxonomy of uncertainty quantification (UQ) for LLMs organised by four mechanistic observation lenses: structural, representational, distributional and semantical. It relates the lenses through the residual stream, orders them by information content, and proposes a principle for choosing UQ methods for different targets.
AI.motivation: Existing UQ taxonomies organise methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism and leave open where in the model's computation uncertainty is observed, which determines what an estimator can recover.
AI.method: Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, the authors define four lenses (structural observes component updates, representational observes hidden states, distributional observes token probabilities, semantical observes distributions over meanings), survey existing methods through them, and separate evaluation targets, criteria and metrics.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experiments; the contributions are the lens framework, the ordering of lenses by information carried, the survey, and a clarification of UQ evaluation protocols.
AI.conclusion: Observation point determines recoverable information, so choosing a UQ method should start from the target and the lens that carries enough information for it, and the paper identifies open problems linking uncertainty estimation to internal computation.

title: SO-Arena: Benchmarking the Capability Spectrum and Reliability of System One Models
comment: 32 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.

AI.tldr: SO-Arena is a benchmark of 11 domains and five capability families for System One models, measuring both capability spectrum and decision reliability through option-set perturbation and missing-answer recognition. Across 21 models, the best-performing model ranks only seventh in reliability, showing that strong overall performance does not imply reliable decisions.
AI.motivation: Aggregate benchmark scores give limited insight into the breadth of System One model capabilities and into whether their decisions are reliable.
AI.method: The benchmark uses evidence-grounded evaluation with verified reference labels, domain-specific difficulty criteria, and interactive sandbox tasks, with System One versus System Two comparison on reasoning-intensive tasks. Reliability is measured by decision stability under controlled option-set changes and by recognition of missing answers when no valid option exists.
AI.result: Across 21 models, the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. The best-performing System One model ranks seventh in reliability.
AI.conclusion: Capability spectrum and decision reliability are complementary dimensions, and both need to be characterised to understand the strengths and limitations of System One models.

title: Computational Explanations of Semantic Universals
comment: submitted to Cambridge Elements in Semantics
summary: Despite their differences, the languages of the world share many deep features when it comes to how they express meaning. These semantic universals are likely to reflect shared aspects of human cognitive, communicative, and social structure. Recent advances in cross-linguistic semantics and computational linguistics allow us to develop explanations of the sources of such properties. This Element presents a body of work doing just that: we explicate a framework for providing computational explanations of semantic universals and then describe several such explanations using principles of ease of learning and efficient communication. Empirical domains include quantifiers, color terms, modals, and indefinites. After providing these explanations, we provide a discussion of future directions for advancing the explanatory power of computational methods in semantic typology.

AI.tldr: This Element presents a framework for computational explanations of semantic universals and applies it to quantifiers, colour terms, modals and indefinites. The explanations rely on principles of ease of learning and efficient communication.
AI.motivation: Languages share deep features in how they express meaning, and these universals are thought to reflect shared aspects of human cognition, communication and social structure, but their sources need explicit explanation.
AI.method: The authors state a framework for computational explanations of semantic universals and build explanations in several empirical domains from principles of learnability and communicative efficiency.
AI.result: The abstract reports no new quantitative results; it describes a body of explanations across quantifiers, colour terms, modals and indefinites.
AI.conclusion: Computational methods can explain semantic universals, and future work should increase their explanatory power in semantic typology.

title: HeriKGQA: Grounded Knowledge-Graph Question Answering over Cultural Heritage Sensor Data
summary: Cultural heritage sites are increasingly monitored by sensor networks, but querying their data requires database expertise. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a natural-language interface, yet over raw sensor records they lose track of which sensor, site, and time each value belongs to, and silently miscompute. We present HeriKGQA, a knowledge-graph question-answering method that confines the LLM to interpreting questions and phrasing answers, leaving computation to SPARQL and deterministic code. Questions are parsed into intents constrained by a heritage ontology aligning W3C SOSA/SSN with CIDOC-CRM, compiled into SPARQL, and answered from query results and temporal, spatial, and anomaly facts derived by a grounding layer, with error correction guarding each LLM step. On 500 questions over real data from five heritage sites, HeriKGQA reaches 99.0% accuracy, 18.2 points above the strongest of three baselines using the same LLM and receiving the same anomaly rules and answer conventions, with comparable answer quality while running almost four times faster. Without grounding, accuracy drops by 12.2 points and on anomaly questions from 99% to 66%. We report lessons from development and live deployment.

AI.tldr: HeriKGQA is a knowledge-graph question-answering method over cultural heritage sensor data that confines the LLM to interpreting questions and phrasing answers, with computation done by SPARQL and deterministic code. On 500 questions from five heritage sites it reaches 99.0% accuracy, 18.2 points above the strongest of three baselines using the same LLM, and runs almost four times faster.
AI.motivation: LLMs offer a natural-language interface to sensor data, but over raw records they lose track of the sensor, site and time of each value and silently miscompute.
AI.method: Questions are parsed into intents constrained by a heritage ontology that aligns W3C SOSA/SSN with CIDOC-CRM, compiled into SPARQL, and answered from query results together with temporal, spatial and anomaly facts derived by a grounding layer. Error correction guards each LLM step.
AI.result: HeriKGQA reaches 99.0% accuracy on 500 real questions, 18.2 points above the strongest baseline, with comparable answer quality and about four times the speed. Without grounding, accuracy drops by 12.2 points, and on anomaly questions it falls from 99% to 66%.
AI.conclusion: Grounding computation in a knowledge graph and deterministic code makes LLM-based sensor querying reliable, and the authors report lessons from development and live deployment.

title: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as primary interfaces for factual retrieval, yet current evaluation paradigms rely almost exclusively on explicit entity names. In this work, we demonstrate that LLM knowledge is fundamentally lexically anchored: models possess extensive factual information but find it significantly difficult to retrieve without explicit name tokens. To quantify this limitation, we introduce ShadowBench, a rigorously hardened, shortcut-resistant benchmark designed to evaluate Latent Entity Association via a novel Dual-Trait Association (DTA) task. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive "Shadow Gap" across all model scales$\unicode{x2013}$up to the frontier models GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6$\unicode{x2013}$where removing lexical anchors causes performance drops of over 20%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this lexical dependency exposes a critical vulnerability in AI safety. Applying ShadowBench to Machine Unlearning, we find that state-of-the-art algorithms (e.g., Gradient Difference, NPO) achieve only superficial lexical erasure. While unlearned models fail on direct queries, our novel Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) metric reveals that for popular entities, models explicitly reconstruct the "forgotten" entity in their internal reasoning traces in over 74% of cases, utilizing residual shadow knowledge to solve associative tasks. Conversely, for niche entities, models retain high shadow accuracy (60-90%) via implicit attribute correlation despite 0% LELR. Ultimately, ShadowBench indicates that current unlearning paradigms create an "Illusion of Forgetting," demonstrating that existing methods act as superficial output filters and are not yet reliable for achieving true parametric erasure.

AI.tldr: ShadowBench evaluates latent entity association with a Dual-Trait Association task and finds a "Shadow Gap" where removing explicit entity names drops performance by over 20% across models, including GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6. Current unlearning methods only superficially erase entities, since unlearned models still reconstruct the forgotten entity in their reasoning traces in over 74% of cases for popular entities.
AI.motivation: Factual retrieval evaluations rely on explicit entity names, which hides whether LLM knowledge is retrievable without lexical anchors and whether unlearning removes it in a deeper sense.
AI.method: The authors introduce ShadowBench, a shortcut-resistant benchmark using a Dual-Trait Association task, and apply it to machine unlearning methods such as Gradient Difference and NPO. They also propose the Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) metric.
AI.result: Removing lexical anchors causes drops of over 20% across model scales. For popular entities, LELR exceeds 74%, and unlearned models reconstruct the forgotten entity internally. For niche entities, shadow accuracy stays at 60-90% with 0% LELR.
AI.conclusion: Current unlearning produces an "Illusion of Forgetting" in which methods act as superficial output filters and are not yet reliable for true parametric erasure.

title: Is Spoken Hungarian Low-resource?: A Quantitative Survey of Hungarian Speech Data Sets
summary: Even though various speech data sets are available in Hungarian, there is a lack of a general overview about their types and sizes. To fill in this gap, we provide a survey of available data sets in spoken Hungarian in five categories (e.g., monolingual, Hungarian part of multilingual, pathological, child-related and dialectal collections). In total, the estimated size of available data is about 2800 hours (across 7500 speakers) and it represents a rich spoken language diversity. However, the distribution of the data and its alignment to real-life (e.g. speech recognition) tasks is far from optimal indicating the need for additional larger-scale natural language speech data sets. Our survey presents an overview of available data sets for Hungarian explaining their strengths and weaknesses which is useful for researchers working on Hungarian across disciplines. In addition, our survey serves as a starting point towards a unified foundational speech model specific to Hungarian.

AI.tldr: A survey of available spoken Hungarian speech datasets in five categories, including monolingual, multilingual, pathological, child-related and dialectal collections. The estimated total is about 2,800 hours across 7,500 speakers, but the distribution and alignment of the data with real tasks such as speech recognition are far from optimal.
AI.motivation: No general overview exists of the types and sizes of Hungarian speech data, which hampers planning for Hungarian speech technology.
AI.method: The authors catalogue and characterise existing Hungarian speech datasets by category and assess their strengths and weaknesses.
AI.result: The estimated size of available data is about 2,800 hours across 7,500 speakers, with rich spoken language diversity. Distribution and task alignment are poor.
AI.conclusion: Hungarian needs larger-scale natural speech datasets, and the survey is a starting point towards a unified foundation speech model for Hungarian.

title: Better Boundary Prediction Does Not Guarantee Better Structural Representation
summary: Punctuation marks often mark phrase boundaries, carrying linguistic information. Therefore, punctuation marks' abundance and feasibility as proxies of linguistic structure has led to suggestions that using punctuation marks to optimise on phrasal structure may help language models (LMs) improve their representations of argument, semantic, and syntactic structures. In this paper, we test the above claim in English across three primary LM architectures: decoder-only, encoder-only, and encoder-decoder LMs, by complementing traditional token prediction with punctuation restoration (PR). Our evidence, collected at the <1B parameter scale, suggests that optimising for boundary prediction does not necessarily guarantee higher-quality structural representation in decoder-only, encoder-decoder, and encoder-only LMs, failing to improve performance on downstream tasks that require understanding structure in linguistic input.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether optimising language models for punctuation restoration improves their structural representations, and finds that it does not: boundary prediction gains do not carry over to better performance on downstream tasks that need structural understanding. The study covers decoder-only, encoder-only and encoder-decoder models below 1B parameters in English.
AI.motivation: Punctuation marks mark phrase boundaries and have been proposed as a proxy for linguistic structure, suggesting that punctuation-based objectives could improve LMs' representations of argument, semantic and syntactic structure.
AI.method: The authors complement token prediction with punctuation restoration across three LM architectures, decoder-only, encoder-only and encoder-decoder, at the sub-1B parameter scale.
AI.result: Optimising for boundary prediction does not necessarily improve structural representation in any of the three architectures and does not improve performance on downstream tasks requiring structural understanding.
AI.conclusion: Better boundary prediction does not guarantee better structural representation, so punctuation restoration should not be assumed to be a useful training signal for structural competence.

title: What Roles Do System Prompts Really Assign? Validating and Steering Occupational Role Vectors in LLMs
comment: 11 pages main text, 35 pages total including references and appendices. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Applications built on large language models assign the model a role through its system prompt, intending to shape how it responds for their use case. We introduce a validation framework for extracting and injecting occupational role vectors, activation-level directions that capture how someone in a given occupational role would distinctively respond to a task or question. We validate these vectors through two complementary lenses, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The interpretability lens asks whether each vector is a stable, separable, domain-consistent representation of its role: extracted vectors are highly reproducible across repeated runs and sampling temperatures, remain separable even for very similar roles, and agree more with themselves across in-domain and out-of-domain questions than with other roles' signal. The control lens asks whether injecting a role vector during generation makes the model express the role, and sustain it over a conversation, as well as a role prompt does. On Qwen, injecting the vector alone makes the model express the intended role substantially more often than unsteered, but at best matches a role prompt; on both models, adding the vector to the prompt strengthens the role in single answers but did not slow the role's decline over 30 turns. Together, the two lenses show why both are needed: out of domain the role is expressed only subtly, yet the activations still encode it; and a vector that is stable and separable can still barely steer the model's behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a validation framework for occupational role vectors, activation-level directions extracted from role system prompts, and tests them on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct through an interpretability lens and a control lens. Vectors are stable and separable, but steering with them barely matches a role prompt and does not stop the role from declining over 30 turns.
AI.motivation: Applications assign roles through system prompts without knowing whether the model's internal representation of a role is stable, separable and actually controllable.
AI.method: Role vectors are extracted from activations and injected during generation. The interpretability lens tests reproducibility across runs and temperatures, separability between similar roles, and domain consistency. The control lens tests whether injection makes the model express the role and sustain it over a conversation, compared against role prompts.
AI.result: Extracted vectors are highly reproducible and separable even for similar roles. On Qwen, injecting the vector alone expresses the intended role substantially more often than the unsteered model but at best matches a role prompt. On both models, adding the vector to the prompt strengthens single answers but does not slow the role's decline over 30 turns. Out of domain the role is expressed only subtly.
AI.conclusion: Both lenses are needed, because a vector can be stable and separable yet barely steer behaviour, and out-of-domain activations still encode the role even when it is not visibly expressed.

title: Human-Likeness and Conversational Preference Diverge for Synthesized Agent Speech in Customer-Service Calls
summary: Listeners can judge an agent's speech on how human it sounds (human-likeness) and on how much they would want to talk to it (conversational preference). Listening tests rarely ask about conversational preference, so the relation between the two judgments is unclear. We compared them in paired-choice tests on 120 turns that actors improvised as customer-service representatives. On each trial, two agents spoke the same turn. In Study 1, both agents came from six commercial text-to-speech systems, each with eight voices. In Study 2, one was the actor's original recording and the other a system. Some systems ranked higher on human-likeness, and others on conversational preference. Listeners chose systems over actors in 19% of human-likeness trials but 36% of conversational preference trials (and 49% for the most preferred system). On both judgments, variation among a system's voices was about three-quarters of that between systems. Of three automatic naturalness scores, two predicted lower human-likeness, and none predicted conversational preference. In this setting, listeners tended to favor faster speech and fewer pauses between clauses on both judgments, and more pitch variation for conversational preference. Thus, measuring only human-likeness or testing one voice per system can misjudge which agents listeners would rather talk to.

AI.tldr: In paired-choice listening tests on 120 improvised customer-service turns, listeners rate human-likeness and conversational preference differently: some text-to-speech systems rank higher on one judgement and others on the other. Listeners chose systems over actors in 19% of human-likeness trials but 36% of conversational preference trials.
AI.motivation: Listening tests rarely ask about conversational preference, so the relation between how human a voice sounds and how much listeners want to talk to it is unclear.
AI.method: Two studies used paired-choice tests on 120 turns improvised by actors as customer-service representatives. Study 1 compared six commercial TTS systems with eight voices each, and Study 2 compared the actor's original recording with a system. Automatic naturalness scores and prosodic features were also analysed.
AI.result: Listeners chose systems over actors in 19% of human-likeness trials and 36% of conversational preference trials, and 49% for the most preferred system. Voice variation within a system was about three-quarters of the variation between systems. Two of three automatic naturalness scores predicted lower human-likeness, and none predicted preference. Listeners favoured faster speech and fewer inter-clause pauses on both judgements, and more pitch variation for preference.
AI.conclusion: Measuring only human-likeness, or testing one voice per system, can misjudge which agents listeners would prefer to talk to.

title: Privileged Information Does Not Guarantee Privileged Guidance: Auditing On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Models
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on next-token targets from a teacher, a frozen copy of the student that additionally receives privileged information, such as a worked solution, hidden from the student. Whether student gains reflect that information remains unclear. Taking the worked solution as privileged information, we audit four stages across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics: Source, whether the teacher can use the solution; Encoding, whether the resulting token targets are useful; Transmission, whether the student learns from the targets; and Expression, whether the student applies the learned behavior without the solution. With the solution, the teacher solves hard problems and recovers from student errors, yet the teacher does not reliably recognize errors, and its token targets do not favor correct trajectories. Repeated training makes successes within the student's reach more frequent rather than unlocking new ones, and corrections the student learns to predict are not reliably expressed in free generation. To isolate the solution's contribution, we vary its availability separately from teacher and student thinking modes. The largest gains occur when a teacher in thinking mode supervises a student trained and evaluated without an explicit thinking trace, and problem-only teachers often match or exceed privileged-solution teachers: the gain tracks the teacher's thinking mode rather than the solution, a pattern we call reasoning arbitrage. Accuracy gains alone therefore do not establish transfer of reasoning from privileged solutions: bottlenecks lie after Source, across Encoding, Transmission, and Expression. Future evaluations must measure what the solution adds to otherwise identical training.

AI.tldr: The paper audits on-policy self-distillation for reasoning models in four stages and finds that privileged worked solutions do not reliably transfer. Gains track the teacher's thinking mode rather than the solution, a pattern the authors call reasoning arbitrage, since problem-only teachers often match or exceed solution-informed teachers.
AI.motivation: On-policy self-distillation trains students on teacher targets built from privileged information, but it is unclear whether the student's gains reflect that information.
AI.method: Using worked solutions as privileged information on mathematics across three Qwen3 scales, the authors audit Source, Encoding, Transmission and Expression stages, and vary solution availability separately from teacher and student thinking modes.
AI.result: The teacher uses the solution to solve hard problems, but it does not reliably recognise errors and its token targets do not favour correct trajectories. Repeated training makes reachable successes more frequent rather than unlocking new ones. The largest gains come from a thinking-mode teacher supervising a student evaluated without thinking traces, and problem-only teachers often match or exceed solution-informed teachers.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy gains alone do not establish transfer of reasoning from privileged solutions, and future evaluations must measure what the solution adds to otherwise identical training.

title: Show Your Work in Swahili: Reinforcement Learning for Native-Language Mathematical Reasoning
summary: We present Fikiria, a two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe for Swahili mathematical reasoning. Its reward multiplies a format gate by a weighted sum of answer accuracy and the ChrF\texttt{++} similarity of the Swahili reasoning to an in-language reference chain of thought, so that training targets the surface fidelity of the reasoning trace and not only the final answer. We train on a 2.3k-problem Swahili dataset created by translating GSM8K with GPT-4.1 and filtering with SSA-COMET. On AfriMGSM Swahili, Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B reaches 79.2\%. Under the same fixed prompt and strict answer-format scoring, GPT-4o reaches 68.0\%, partly because it often fails the required answer format; IrokoBench reports 78.8\% for GPT-4o using a best-per-model prompt, a figure numerically close to ours but not directly comparable. In a small human evaluation with co-author annotators, GPT-4o's outputs were preferred overall. ChrF\texttt{++} measures surface fidelity, not the validity of individual reasoning steps.

AI.tldr: Fikiria is a two-stage SFT plus GRPO recipe for Swahili mathematical reasoning whose reward multiplies a format gate by accuracy and ChrF++ similarity to a Swahili reference reasoning chain. On AfriMGSM Swahili, the Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B model reaches 79.2%, against 68.0% for GPT-4o under the same fixed prompt and strict format scoring.
AI.motivation: Models are typically judged on final answers, so they may produce reasoning in low-resource languages that is not faithful in surface form, and training should target the fidelity of the reasoning trace as well.
AI.method: The authors train on a 2.3k-problem Swahili dataset made by translating GSM8K with GPT-4.1 and filtering with SSA-COMET. The reward combines a format gate with weighted answer accuracy and ChrF++ similarity to an in-language reference chain of thought.
AI.result: Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B reaches 79.2% on AfriMGSM Swahili. Under the same fixed prompt and strict answer-format scoring GPT-4o reaches 68.0%, partly because it often fails the format. IrokoBench reports 78.8% for GPT-4o with a best-per-model prompt, which is not directly comparable. In a small human evaluation GPT-4o's outputs were preferred overall.
AI.conclusion: Rewarding surface fidelity of native-language reasoning can help mathematical reasoning in Swahili, but ChrF++ does not measure whether individual reasoning steps are valid.

title: Temporal Context-Aware Spam Detection Using Transformer-Based NLP Models
summary: Spam detection is usually treated as single-message classification, ignoring behavioral patterns that emerge across sequences of messages from the same sender. We study outbound SMS spam detection at the carrier level, where the goal is to predict at send time whether a carrier will flag a message as spam. Using a proprietary production database of 43,741 outbound SMS messages with UTC transmission timestamps and carrier delivery statuses, we report three sets of results. On an 8,749-message held-out test set, a TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline reaches AUC-ROC 0.8721, and a text-only DeBERTa-v3-base classifier reaches AUC-ROC 0.9011 and F1 0.8412. A deployed DistilBERT model augmented with inter-message temporal features reaches accuracy 0.8238, spam-class F1 0.8382, and recall 0.9128 at threshold 0.5 on a separate, class-balanced 20,000-message production evaluation set; these results are not directly comparable with the held-out test results. We also describe TemporalBertSpam, an architecture that encodes each sender's message history with a causal Transformer, and outline the same-split evaluation needed to measure its contribution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies outbound SMS spam detection at the carrier level, predicting at send time whether a carrier will flag a message as spam, and shows that a DistilBERT model with inter-message temporal features is deployed. On a 43,741-message production database, a DeBERTa-v3 text-only model reaches AUC-ROC 0.9011 on a held-out test set, and the paper proposes TemporalBertSpam for sender history modelling.
AI.motivation: Spam detection is usually treated as single-message classification, which ignores behavioural patterns across a sender's sequence of messages.
AI.method: The authors compare a TF-IDF plus logistic regression baseline and a text-only DeBERTa-v3-base classifier on a held-out test set, and a deployed DistilBERT model augmented with inter-message temporal features on a separate class-balanced evaluation set. They also describe TemporalBertSpam, which encodes each sender's history with a causal Transformer.
AI.result: On the 8,749-message held-out test set, TF-IDF plus logistic regression reaches AUC-ROC 0.8721, and DeBERTa-v3-base reaches AUC-ROC 0.9011 and F1 0.8412. The deployed DistilBERT model reaches accuracy 0.8238, spam-class F1 0.8382 and recall 0.9128 at threshold 0.5 on a separate 20,000-message evaluation set, which is not directly comparable with the held-out results. TemporalBertSpam is not yet evaluated on the same split.
AI.conclusion: Temporal context helps predict carrier spam flagging in production, but the paper leaves the contribution of TemporalBertSpam to a same-split evaluation still to be done.

title: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features
summary: Existing large language models typically rely on massive fine-tuning datasets for safety alignment, which results in higher costs for safety alignment and often leads to the problem of over-refusal. We propose Less is Safer (LIS), a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment, constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. Specifically, we leverage Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) activations to efficiently select prompts that cover diverse and interpretable safety features. Then, we employ a multi-agent adversarial synthesis framework to generate harmless prompts that nevertheless elicit unnecessary refusals. LIS contains only 2.4K samples, yet outperforms much larger datasets, e.g., TRIDENT-Core (26K), TRIDENT-Edge (19K) and WildJailbreak (262K), in overall performance on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. Through ablation experiments, we demonstrate that neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone can achieve optimal results. We also used safety features from SAE, annotated by an LLM, for data filtering, but the results were inferior to those obtained using the pipeline proposed in this paper.

AI.tldr: LIS (Less is Safer) is a compact 2.4K-sample safety alignment dataset built from SAE-guided prompt selection and multi-agent adversarial synthesis of harmless prompts that still trigger unnecessary refusals. It outperforms much larger datasets, such as WildJailbreak with 262K samples, on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment usually relies on massive fine-tuning datasets, which are costly and often cause over-refusal of harmless requests.
AI.method: Sparse Autoencoder activations select prompts that cover diverse, interpretable safety features, and a multi-agent adversarial framework generates harmless prompts that elicit unnecessary refusals. Ablations compare safety data and over-refusal data.
AI.result: LIS, with 2.4K samples, outperforms TRIDENT-Core (26K), TRIDENT-Edge (19K) and WildJailbreak (262K) overall on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. Neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone achieves the best results. SAE features annotated by an LLM for filtering give inferior results.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable feature-guided selection with adversarial over-refusal data gives a cheap and effective safety alignment dataset, and the proposed pipeline outperforms LLM-annotated SAE feature filtering.

title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue
comment: Zhicheng Jia, Shuchen Wu, and Zhuoshi Tong contributed equally to this work
summary: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MindMem is a memory framework for long-term character dialogue that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into mental states of the character, the user and their relationship, and uses a mental-state reasoner to recover relationally important episodes. On MemReal-Bench it reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 points.
AI.motivation: Conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over fact stores, retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences.
AI.method: Inspired by the Self-Memory System, MindMem consolidates shared experiences asynchronously into source-linked mental states. At each turn a mental-state reasoner anticipates latent user needs, forms proactive intentions and retrieves supporting episodic evidence. MemReal-Bench pairs Direct Question Answering with Situated Memory Realization across month-long real-user interactions in dyadic and group scenes.
AI.result: MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, and outperforms oracle target-memory injection on SMR.
AI.conclusion: Agents must do more than recall facts, and using mental-state consolidation to make shared history shape behaviour improves situated memory use beyond factual question answering.

title: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted at the GlobalSouthAI Workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: We run reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO across four environments, starting from a supervised fine-tuned 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model covering English and eight Indic languages. We compare the model before and after RL across 34 benchmarks in one evaluation campaign. MATH improves by 36.07 points, and most Indic benchmarks also improve. Yet XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points as English answers rise from 8.7% to 91.7%; IndicQA falls 8.64, while English XQuAD gains 11.71 F1. A second RL run from the same supervised initialization adds an Indic environment together with language and repetition rewards. Compared with the released model, it improves both passage-answering and instruction-following benchmarks, along with preserving MATH performance. But it loses ground on reasoning and coding benchmarks. Several training choices changed together, so we cannot isolate the effect of any one of the reward terms. Script compliance remains unresolved. Adding a language reward did not ensure use of the requested script. Passage answering and script compliance therefore need direct evaluation, even when other benchmark scores improve.

AI.tldr: Reinforcement learning with GRPO on a supervised 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model covering English and eight Indic languages improves MATH by 36.07 points and most Indic benchmarks, but XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points as English answers rise from 8.7% to 91.7%. A second run adding an Indic environment and language and repetition rewards improves passage answering and instruction following, but loses ground on reasoning and coding.
AI.motivation: RL improvements can come with regressions on the language and script behaviour users need, and this needs to be measured across a broad benchmark suite.
AI.method: The authors run GRPO across four environments and compare the model before and after RL across 34 benchmarks in one evaluation campaign. A second RL run from the same initialisation adds an Indic environment with language and repetition rewards.
AI.result: MATH improves by 36.07 points and most Indic benchmarks improve, but XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points, IndicQA falls 8.64, and English XQuAD gains 11.71 F1. The second run improves passage answering and instruction following relative to the released model and preserves MATH, but loses ground on reasoning and coding. Script compliance is unresolved, and a language reward did not ensure use of the requested script.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark gains can hide regressions in passage answering and script compliance, so these need direct evaluation even when other scores improve.

title: Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text
summary: A multilingual speech recogniser has heard much speech in its own languages. We ask how much of that it brings to a language it was never trained on, when it is fine-tuned on the little that language has. We score 28 open multilingual models untouched on Low-Language-TTS, 50 low-resource languages in 11 writing systems, and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips a language, 82 hours in all, with a dev set choosing every epoch. Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate (CER), by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, and a word language model takes three CTC models 1.2 to 1.4 points lower; WER is still 34.4 at best. On the 12 languages that no model lists, every model starts at 46 or worse and the best ends at 11.7. The same architectures from random weights stay 60 points or more behind, so the gain is transfer, and an encoder left untouched already gives a Whisper or Qwen decoder most of what it needs. It is the language, not the corpus: on FLEURS recordings that ours do not share, the median model keeps 79% of its gain. It costs the languages the models knew, 5.7 points of CER on English, Spanish, French and German in the median model. Low-rank adapters on 4% of the weights come within 1.1 points of tuning everything, and on 2 of 3 models forget less. Seq2seq and language-model decoders are done within three to five epochs, while a new CTC head is still improving at twenty or thirty. Data beats epochs: 25 clips a language take Qwen3-ASR 0.6B from 60.9 to 39.3, and at equal clips presented, ten times the data is worth 9.7 points. A model that first learned forty of the languages learns the other ten no faster. On a public Malay benchmark, untouched Whisper large-v3 scores 8.9 when it detects the language and 14.9 when told the clip is Malay, because it then translates the English that speakers mix in; trained on the Scicom telephony dataset it scores 6.0.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates 28 open multilingual speech recognisers on 50 low-resource languages and fine-tunes 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips per language, finding that fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best. The gains are largely transfer, not data memorisation, and low-rank adapters on 4% of weights come within 1.1 points of full tuning.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how much a multilingual speech model's prior knowledge helps a language it was never trained on when only a small amount of data is available.
AI.method: The authors score 28 models untouched on Low-Language-TTS (50 languages in 11 writing systems) and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips per language (82 hours in total), choosing the epoch with a dev set. They compare against random initialisation, test on FLEURS, and compare LoRA with full tuning.
AI.result: Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro CER by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, while WER remains 34.4 at best. Random-weight models stay 60 points or more behind. On FLEURS the median model keeps 79% of its gain. The median model loses 5.7 CER points on English, Spanish, French and German. Adapters on 4% of weights come within 1.1 points of full tuning. Seq2seq and LM decoders converge in three to five epochs, while new CTC heads keep improving at twenty or thirty.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained multilingual speech models transfer well to unseen low-resource languages, and data quantity matters more than the number of epochs, though fine-tuning can cost performance on the languages the models already knew.

title: Label-Efficient Document-Grounded Factuality Detection via Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent claims that are unsupported by a given source document, motivating accurate and efficient document-grounded factuality detection. Existing LLM-based evaluators often require repeated inference and incur high computational cost, whereas compact factuality detectors are efficient at inference time but commonly rely on large labeled or synthetically generated corpora. We propose CPIL (Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning), a two-stage Siamese framework that converts a small labeled set into relational supervision without acquiring additional factuality labels. CPIL constructs positive pairs from distinct label-preserving paraphrastic views of the same document-claim instance and negative pairs from opposite-label examples associated with the same source document. It further introduces quantile-aware semi-hard negative mining, which derives a boundary from the positive-pair similarity distribution and balances informative negatives with broader coverage. In the two-stage training procedure, Stage 1 learns an encoder from these task-aware pairs, and Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the encoder and a linear classification head for binary factuality prediction. At inference time, CPIL requires no paraphrase generation, pair construction, or Siamese comparison and uses only one encoder-classifier forward pass. On the 11-task LLM-AggreFact benchmark, CPIL-2% and CPIL-3% achieve macro-F1 scores of 81.04 and 81.60 while using only 2-3% of the FactCG-released labeled pool. Both settings outperform all compared compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references. Ablations and sensitivity analyses support the contributions of task-aware pair construction, dynamic negative mining, and multi-pivot paraphrasing.

AI.tldr: CPIL is a two-stage Siamese framework that turns a small labelled set into relational supervision through paraphrase-invariant positive pairs and quantile-aware semi-hard negative mining, and uses a single encoder-classifier pass at inference. With 2-3% of the FactCG labelled pool it reaches macro-F1 of 81.04 and 81.60 on the 11-task LLM-AggreFact benchmark, outperforming compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references.
AI.motivation: LLM-based factuality evaluators are costly at inference, while compact detectors need large labelled or synthetic corpora, so there is a need for label-efficient document-grounded factuality detection.
AI.method: Stage 1 learns an encoder from positive pairs (distinct label-preserving paraphrases of the same document-claim instance) and negative pairs (opposite-label examples from the same document), with negatives mined using a boundary derived from the positive-pair similarity distribution. Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the encoder and a linear head for binary factuality prediction.
AI.result: CPIL-2% and CPIL-3% achieve macro-F1 of 81.04 and 81.60 on LLM-AggreFact using 2-3% of the labelled pool. Both outperform all compared compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references. Ablations support task-aware pair construction, dynamic negative mining and multi-pivot paraphrasing.
AI.conclusion: Relational supervision from a small labelled set can produce efficient factuality detectors that match or beat larger compact models, without paraphrase generation or Siamese comparison at inference.

title: SMIC: Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning across Transformer Layers for Natural Language Inference
summary: Natural Language Inference models can be sensitive to localized lexical changes. We introduce Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning (SMIC), which constructs a single input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across Transformer layers. Each layer applies its own multiscale transformation to the shared reference and injects the resulting conditioning feature before the attention update. We instantiate SMIC in a token--context Transformer (TCT) and conduct from-scratch comparisons against decoder-based and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines across all three ANLI rounds. TCT-SMIC attains the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds. The ablations further support the contribution of SMIC. We evaluate a real-valued Llama-style plug-in and extend deletion/insertion diagnostics to pretrained ModernBERT encoder and Llama decoder models with and without SMIC. Across the evaluated perturbation protocols, TCT-SMIC exhibits comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes. We further establish a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution in terms of the mean Jensen--Shannon divergence between the restricted and renormalized attention distributions.

AI.tldr: SMIC (Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning) builds one input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across all Transformer layers, with each layer conditioning its attention on it. The TCT-SMIC model achieves the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds, and the paper proves a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution.
AI.motivation: NLI models can be sensitive to localised lexical changes, and the authors seek a conditioning mechanism that stabilises attention against such perturbations.
AI.method: SMIC applies a per-layer multiscale transformation to a shared reference and injects the result before the attention update.
